name: Shannon Entropy (Binary)
description: Gives the Shannon entropy of a binary (two-outcome) source with success probability p, computed as -p*log2(p)-(1-p)*log2(1-p). It measures the average information content, or uncertainty, in bits per symbol.
notes: p must be between 0 and 1, with terms at p = 0 or 1 taken as zero. Entropy peaks at 1 bit when p = 0.5 and falls to 0 when the outcome is certain.

name: Self-Information (Surprisal)
description: Gives the self-information (surprisal) of an event with probability p, computed as -log2(p) in bits. Rarer events carry more information, so a lower probability yields a larger surprisal.
notes: p must be strictly between 0 and 1; a certain event (p = 1) has zero surprisal. Using log base 2 gives bits, while natural log would give nats.

name: Shannon-Hartley Capacity (SNR in dB)
description: Gives the Shannon-Hartley channel capacity in bits per second, computed as B*log2(1+10^(snr_db/10)) from bandwidth B and signal-to-noise ratio snr_db in decibels. It is the maximum error-free data rate of the channel.
notes: The SNR is given in dB and converted to a linear ratio via 10^(snr_db/10). B is in hertz; the result is a theoretical upper bound assuming additive white Gaussian noise.

name: Nats to Bits Conversion
description: Converts an information quantity expressed in nats (natural-log units) into bits by dividing by ln(2). One nat equals about 1.4427 bits, so the result rescales the same information content to a base-2 measure.
notes: Only changes the logarithm base of an information measure; it does not alter the underlying entropy. Use the inverse (multiply bits by ln(2)) to go from bits back to nats.

name: Binary Symmetric Channel Capacity
description: Gives the channel capacity of a binary symmetric channel, equal to 1 minus the binary entropy of the crossover probability p. It is the maximum reliable information per channel use, in bits, when each bit is flipped with probability p.
notes: p is a probability between 0 and 1; capacity is 1 bit at p=0 or p=1 and drops to 0 at p=0.5. The formula assumes an ideal memoryless channel with independent bit flips.

name: Binary Erasure Channel Capacity
description: Gives the capacity of a binary erasure channel as 1 minus the erasure probability. Each transmitted bit is either received correctly or lost (erased) with probability eps, so a fraction 1-eps of bits gets through on average.
notes: eps is a probability from 0 to 1. Unlike a symmetric channel, erased bits are known to be missing rather than silently flipped, which is why the capacity is simply the fraction of surviving bits.

name: Kullback-Leibler Divergence (Bernoulli)
description: Computes the Kullback-Leibler divergence in bits between two Bernoulli distributions with success probabilities p (true) and q (model). It measures how many extra bits are needed on average when coding samples from p using a code optimized for q.
notes: Not symmetric: swapping p and q gives a different value. It is zero only when p equals q and diverges if q is 0 or 1 while p is not. p and q must lie strictly between 0 and 1.

name: Cross-Entropy (Binary)
description: Computes the binary cross-entropy in bits between a true probability p and a predicted probability q. It is the average number of bits needed to encode outcomes drawn from p using a code based on q, and is minimized when q equals p.
notes: Cross-entropy equals the entropy of p plus the KL divergence from p to q, so it is at least the entropy of p. q must be strictly between 0 and 1 to avoid an infinite value.

name: Perplexity from Entropy
description: Converts an entropy H measured in bits into perplexity, defined as 2 raised to the power H. Perplexity represents the effective number of equally likely choices a source or model faces, giving an intuitive branching factor.
notes: H must be entropy expressed in bits (base-2) for this exponent; if entropy is in nats, use e^H instead. Higher perplexity means more uncertainty.

name: Code Redundancy
description: Measures the relative redundancy of a source as 1 minus the ratio of actual entropy H to the maximum possible entropy log2(N) of an alphabet of N symbols. It indicates the fraction of capacity that is wasted by non-uniform or predictable symbols.
notes: H must be in bits and not exceed log2(N). A value of 0 means the source is maximally efficient (uniform), while values near 1 indicate highly redundant, compressible data.

name: Source Efficiency (Entropy Ratio)
description: Computes source efficiency as the ratio of actual entropy H to the maximum entropy log2(N) for an N-symbol alphabet. It is the complement of redundancy and shows how close the source is to using its symbols with equal, fully informative probability.
notes: H must be in bits and at most log2(N), giving a result between 0 and 1. Efficiency of 1 means a perfectly uniform, incompressible source.

name: Code Rate (Block Code)
description: Gives the code rate of a block code as the number of information bits k divided by the total code word length n. It expresses the fraction of each transmitted word that carries payload rather than redundancy for error control.
notes: Requires k not greater than n, giving a rate between 0 and 1. The remaining fraction 1-k/n is redundancy added by n-k parity bits.

name: Coding Efficiency (Entropy per Symbol Length)
description: Computes coding efficiency as source entropy H divided by the average code length L, both in bits. It shows how close a variable-length code comes to the theoretical minimum average length set by the source entropy.
notes: By the source coding theorem L cannot be less than H, so efficiency is at most 1; a value near 1 means an almost optimal code. Both H and L must be expressed in bits.

name: Hamming Bound Redundancy (Single-Error)
description: Gives the minimum number of parity (redundancy) bits needed for a single-error-correcting code of code word length n, as log2(1+n). It follows from the Hamming bound, which requires enough check bits to uniquely identify any single-bit error position or the no-error case.
notes: The true number of parity bits is the ceiling of this value since bits are integers; the formula gives the exact bound only when n+1 is a power of two. n is the full code word length in bits.

name: Eb/N0 from SNR
description: Converts a linear signal-to-noise ratio into energy-per-bit to noise-density ratio Eb/N0 by multiplying SNR by the bandwidth B and dividing by the bit rate R. It normalizes signal quality per information bit rather than per unit bandwidth.
notes: SNR and the result are linear ratios, not decibels. The relation assumes noise power equals N0 times B; convert the result to dB with 10*log10 if needed.

name: Shannon Limit Eb/N0 (Spectral Efficiency)
description: Computes the minimum linear Eb/N0 required to communicate reliably at a given spectral efficiency eta, using the Shannon capacity bound (2^eta - 1)/eta. It marks the theoretical energy-efficiency limit for a target bits-per-second-per-hertz.
notes: The result is a linear ratio; as eta approaches 0 it tends to ln(2) (about -1.59 dB), the ultimate Shannon limit. No practical code can operate below this bound.

name: Spectral Efficiency
description: Computes spectral efficiency as the bit rate R divided by the bandwidth B, giving how many bits per second are transmitted in each hertz of bandwidth. It quantifies how effectively a system uses its allotted spectrum.
notes: R is in bits per second and B in hertz, yielding units of bit/s/Hz. Higher values require higher-order modulation and better SNR to keep errors acceptable.

name: Processing Gain (Spread Spectrum)
description: Computes the processing gain of a spread-spectrum system in decibels as 10 times the base-10 log of the spread bandwidth divided by the data rate. It quantifies the interference and jamming rejection gained by spreading the signal over a wider band.
notes: Here log is base-10 and the result is in dB. Both bw and R must use consistent units; the ratio bw/R equals the spreading factor.

name: Signal-to-Noise Ratio (dB)
description: Converts a linear power ratio into decibels as 10 times its base-10 logarithm. It expresses how many times larger the signal power is than the noise power on the logarithmic dB scale used throughout communications and audio engineering.
notes: Use factor 10 because the input is a power ratio; for an amplitude or voltage ratio use factor 20 instead. The input must be a positive linear ratio, not already in dB.

name: Quantization SNR (SQNR)
description: Estimates the signal-to-quantization-noise ratio in decibels for an ideal n-bit uniform quantizer as 6.02*n + 1.76. Each additional bit adds about 6 dB, reflecting the halving of quantization step size and its noise.
notes: The 1.76 dB constant assumes a full-scale sinusoidal input; other signal statistics shift this offset. The result is an ideal upper bound ignoring other noise sources.

name: Quantizer Step Size
description: Computes the step size (least significant bit value) of a uniform quantizer as the full-scale range vfs divided by 2 to the power n, the number of quantization levels. It is the smallest voltage difference the quantizer can distinguish.
notes: Uses 2^n levels for the full-scale range; some conventions divide by (2^n - 1) instead. vfs and the result share the same voltage unit.

name: Quantization Noise Power
description: Computes the mean-square quantization noise power as the square of the quantization step delta divided by 12. This is the variance of the uniformly distributed rounding error introduced by an ideal quantizer.
notes: Assumes the quantization error is uniformly distributed over one step and uncorrelated with the signal. The result is a power in squared volts; take its square root for RMS noise.

name: Differential Entropy (Gaussian)
description: Computes the differential entropy in bits of a Gaussian distribution with standard deviation sigma, as 0.5*log2(2*pi*e*sigma^2). It measures the spread of a continuous normal variable on a base-2 scale.
notes: Differential entropy of continuous variables can be negative when sigma is small, unlike discrete entropy. sigma is the standard deviation, and the result is in bits because a base-2 log is used.

name: Differential Entropy (Continuous Uniform)
description: Computes the differential entropy in bits of a continuous uniform distribution on the interval [a, b], as the base-2 log of the width b-a. It reflects how much continuous uncertainty a flat distribution over that range carries.
notes: Requires b greater than a so the width is positive. The value is negative when the interval is narrower than 1 unit, which is normal for differential entropy.

name: Differential Entropy (Exponential)
description: Computes the differential entropy in nats of an exponential distribution with rate parameter lam, as 1 - ln(lam). It quantifies the continuous uncertainty of waiting-time or lifetime distributions on a natural-log scale.
notes: The result is in nats because a natural log is used; multiply by 1/ln(2) for bits. lam is the rate (inverse mean) and must be positive; larger lam gives lower entropy.

name: Mutual Information (Entropy Difference)
description: Computes the mutual information between input and output as the output entropy H(Y) minus the conditional entropy H(Y|X). It is the average amount of information, in bits, that the output reveals about the input.
notes: Both entropies must be in bits; mutual information is symmetric and cannot be negative, so H(Y|X) never exceeds H(Y). A value of 0 means input and output are independent.

name: Renyi Collision Entropy (Binary)
description: Computes the Renyi collision entropy (order 2) in bits of a binary source with probabilities p and 1-p, as minus the log2 of the collision probability p^2 + (1-p)^2. It reflects the likelihood that two independent draws coincide.
notes: This order-2 Renyi entropy is at most the Shannon entropy and equals 1 bit only when p=0.5. p is a probability between 0 and 1.

name: Min-Entropy (Binary Source)
description: Computes the min-entropy in bits of a binary source as minus the log2 of the larger of the two outcome probabilities. It captures the worst-case unpredictability, driven by the most likely outcome, and is key to security guarantees.
notes: Min-entropy is the smallest of the Renyi entropies and never exceeds the Shannon entropy. p is a probability between 0 and 1; the result reaches 1 bit only at p=0.5.

name: Tsallis Entropy (Binary)
description: Computes the Tsallis entropy of a binary source with probability p and entropic index q, as (1 - (p^q + (1-p)^q))/(q-1). It is a non-extensive generalization of entropy used in complex and non-equilibrium systems.
notes: q must not equal 1 to avoid division by zero; as q approaches 1 it converges to the Shannon entropy (in nats). p is a probability between 0 and 1.

name: AWGN Capacity per Dimension
description: Computes the Shannon capacity per dimension of an additive white Gaussian noise channel as 0.5*log2(1+snr). It is the maximum bits per real signal dimension (or per channel use) at a given linear signal-to-noise ratio.
notes: snr is a linear power ratio, not decibels. The factor 0.5 gives capacity per real dimension; a complex channel with two dimensions has double this value, log2(1+snr).

name: Landauer Limit (Minimum Erasure Energy)
description: Computes the Landauer limit, the minimum energy in joules that must be dissipated to erase one bit of information, as the Boltzmann constant times temperature times ln(2). It sets a fundamental thermodynamic floor on irreversible computation.
notes: Temperature must be absolute (kelvin); the limit rises with temperature. At room temperature this is only about 3e-21 J, far below the energy real logic gates actually use.

name: Thermal Noise Power (kTB)
description: Computes the available thermal (Johnson-Nyquist) noise power in watts as Boltzmann constant times absolute temperature times bandwidth. It gives the fundamental noise floor a receiver faces over a given bandwidth.
notes: Temperature is in kelvin and bandwidth in hertz; the result is available noise power into a matched load. Convert to dBm with 10*log10(power/1e-3).

name: Noise Factor from Noise Figure
description: Converts a noise figure given in decibels into the linear noise factor as 10 raised to the power nf/10. The noise factor is the linear ratio by which a device degrades the signal-to-noise ratio.
notes: Noise figure is the dB form and noise factor is the linear form of the same quantity; a 0 dB figure gives a factor of 1 (ideal, noiseless). nf must be the value in dB.

name: Space Saving (Compression)
description: Computes the space saving of compression as 1 minus the ratio of compressed size c to original size o. It expresses the fraction of storage eliminated, so 0.7 means the compressed data is 70 percent smaller than the original.
notes: c and o must use the same size unit; the value is positive when compression shrinks the data and negative if the output is larger. This differs from the compression ratio o/c.

name: BPSK Bit Error Rate (Approximation)
description: Gives an exponential approximation of the bit error rate for BPSK modulation as 0.5*exp(-ebn0), where ebn0 is the linear energy-per-bit to noise-density ratio. It estimates the probability that a received bit is decoded incorrectly.
notes: This is a Chernoff-type upper-bound approximation, not the exact Q-function result, and is loosest at low Eb/N0. ebn0 must be a linear ratio, not decibels.

name: Bit Rate from Symbol Rate (M-ary)
description: Computes the bit rate in bits per second by multiplying the symbol (baud) rate by the number of bits per symbol log2(M), where M is the number of distinct symbols. It converts a modulation's symbol rate into its actual data throughput.
notes: baud is the symbol rate and M the constellation size; log2(M) is an integer only when M is a power of two. Bit rate exceeds baud rate whenever more than one bit rides on each symbol.
